subject: dbms
title: Unit 4 — Textbook Exercises (Elmasri/Navathe Ch20–24, Silberschatz Ch17–18)

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 17.5)** Since every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable, why do we emphasise conflict serializability rather than view serializability?
options: Conflict serializability can be tested efficiently (precedence-graph cycle check), whereas testing view serializability is NP-complete
items.explain: View serializability captures more schedules but testing it is NP-complete; conflict serializability is a cheap cycle check, so practical protocols (2PL) enforce it.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.12 / Elmasri Review 20.6)** Which set correctly lists the ACID properties of a transaction?
items.explain: ACID = Atomicity (all-or-none), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (appear to run alone), Durability (committed changes persist).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.13)** A transaction passes through several states until it commits or aborts. Which is a valid state sequence?
items.explain: A successful transaction goes active → partially committed (checks run) → committed. A failing one goes active → failed → aborted → terminated.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.14 / Elmasri Review 20.9)** What distinguishes a serial schedule from a serializable schedule?
options: A serial schedule has NO interleaving (one transaction at a time); a serializable schedule interleaves but is equivalent to some serial schedule
A serializable schedule is always inconsistent
items.explain: Serial = no concurrency. Serializable = concurrent but equivalent in effect to a serial schedule, giving the same consistency with better throughput.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.17)** A recoverable schedule is one in which:
options: A transaction commits only after every transaction whose changes it read has committed
items.explain: Recoverability ensures a committed transaction never needs to be undone: if Tj read from Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj. Otherwise Ti's abort would force undoing a committed Tj.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.7)** A cascadeless schedule is desirable because:
options: Transactions read only committed values, so an abort never forces other transactions to abort (no cascading rollback)
items.explain: In a cascadeless schedule every read is of committed data, so aborting one transaction cannot cascade aborts to others that read its uncommitted writes.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.18)** Why do database systems support concurrent execution despite the extra effort to keep it correct?
options: For improved throughput/resource utilisation and reduced waiting time
items.explain: Concurrency improves CPU and disk utilisation (one transaction uses the CPU while another waits on I/O) and reduces average response time — worth the cost of concurrency control.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.8)** The lost update anomaly occurs when Tj reads an item, Tk writes it, and then:
options: Tj writes the item (ignoring Tk's value), so Tk's update is lost
Both commit successfully with no conflict
items.explain: Lost update: Tj's later write, based on the value it read before Tk's update, overwrites Tk's update, which is lost. It is possible under READ COMMITTED but not REPEATABLE READ.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.3)** Why have database-system implementers paid much more attention to the ACID properties than file-system implementers?
options: Databases manage shared, concurrent, critical data where partial updates and concurrency anomalies would corrupt integrity, so atomicity/isolation/durability are essential
ACID does not apply to files
items.explain: Databases serve many concurrent users updating interrelated, critical data; without ACID, concurrent or partial updates would violate integrity. File systems handle mostly independent, less-constrained data.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.1)** Is a recovery manager required for a database system that NEVER fails?
options: No — recovery (atomicity/durability via undo/redo) is needed precisely to cope with failures; with no failures it would be unnecessary
items.explain: The recovery manager exists to restore consistency after failures. If a system genuinely never failed, recovery would not be needed (concurrency control still would, for isolation).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 17.19)** Why does the READ COMMITTED isolation level ensure schedules are cascade-free?
options: Because transactions read only committed data, so no transaction reads another's uncommitted write — so an abort cannot cascade
It holds all locks till commit
items.explain: READ COMMITTED never reads uncommitted data, so no transaction depends on another's uncommitted writes; aborting one cannot force cascading aborts of others.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 20.22)** To determine whether a schedule like `r1(X); r3(X); w1(X); r2(X); w3(X)` is conflict serializable, you:
options: Build the precedence graph from conflicts and check for a cycle (acyclic ⇒ serializable, with serial order from a topological sort)
items.explain: List conflicts, draw edges Ti→Tj, and test for cycles. No cycle ⇒ conflict serializable, and the topological order gives the equivalent serial schedule.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 20.23)** When you draw the serializability (precedence) graph for a schedule and it contains a cycle, the schedule is:
options: View serializable but not conflict serializable
items.explain: A cycle in the precedence graph means no consistent serial order exists, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. An acyclic graph yields the equivalent serial schedule(s).

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 20.8)** What is the difference between conflict equivalence and view equivalence of schedules?
options: Conflict equivalence requires the same order of conflicting operations; view equivalence requires the same initial reads, read-from relationships, and final writes
items.explain: Conflict equivalence is based on the relative order of conflicting operations; view equivalence is based on read-from relationships and final writes. Conflict-equivalent ⇒ view-equivalent, not vice-versa.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 20.13)** A phantom violation specifically refers to:
options: Re-reading a row and getting a different value
A newly inserted row appearing in a re-executed range/WHERE query that was not there before
items.explain: A phantom is a new row (matching a WHERE condition) inserted by another transaction, appearing in a re-run query. Dirty read = uncommitted data; non-repeatable read = a changed value.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 20.20)** Why does SQL need an explicit transaction END (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) statement but not an explicit BEGIN?
options: A transaction begins implicitly with the first executable statement, but the system needs an explicit COMMIT/ROLLBACK to know when the unit of work is finished
items.explain: The first statement implicitly starts a transaction, so no BEGIN is required; but the DBMS cannot guess where the transaction ends, so an explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK is mandatory.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 21.1)** How does the two-phase locking protocol guarantee serializability?
options: By splitting locking into a growing phase (acquire only) and a shrinking phase (release only), so transactions serialize in lock-point order
items.explain: 2PL's two-phase rule (all locks acquired before any is released) makes the precedence graph acyclic — transactions serialize in the order of their lock points — guaranteeing conflict serializability.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 21.2)** Why is strict or rigorous two-phase locking often preferred over basic 2PL?
options: It additionally guarantees recoverable, cascadeless (strict) schedules by holding locks until commit/abort
items.explain: Basic 2PL gives conflict serializability but can allow cascading rollback. Strict 2PL (hold X-locks till commit) / rigorous 2PL (hold all locks till commit) ensure recoverable, cascadeless schedules.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 21.20)** The proof that basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability uses the idea that if the serializability graph had a cycle, then:
options: At least one transaction must have acquired a lock AFTER releasing one — violating the two-phase rule
items.explain: A cycle would require a transaction to lock after unlocking, contradicting 2PL's growing-then-shrinking rule. Hence 2PL schedules have acyclic graphs and are conflict serializable.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 21.3)** Deadlock and starvation are two problems with locking. Deadlock is when:
options: A transaction waits forever for a continuous stream of other locks
Two or more transactions each wait for a lock held by another, so none can proceed
items.explain: Deadlock = a cycle of waiting (each transaction waits for a lock another holds). Starvation = a transaction is repeatedly bypassed and never gets its lock; both are distinct locking problems.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 21.4)** Why are shared/exclusive locks preferable to simple binary locks?
options: They allow multiple readers concurrently (shared mode), increasing concurrency, while still serialising writers (exclusive mode)
items.explain: A binary lock allows only one transaction per item (read or write). Shared/exclusive locks let many transactions read concurrently and restrict only writing — much higher concurrency.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 21.5)** The wait-die and wound-wait protocols are techniques for:
options: Deadlock prevention (using transaction timestamps to decide whether a transaction waits or is rolled back)
items.explain: Wait-die and wound-wait are timestamp-based deadlock-PREVENTION schemes: based on which transaction is older, a requesting transaction either waits or is aborted, ensuring no cyclic wait can form.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 24.2)** Which correctly pairs a NoSQL category with an example system?
options: Key-value → DynamoDB; Graph → Neo4j; Document → MongoDB; Wide-column → Cassandra
items.explain: The four categories and examples: document (MongoDB, CouchDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, HBase), graph (Neo4j).

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 24.5)** Of the three CAP properties, which two are typically emphasised by NoSQL systems?
options: Availability and Partition tolerance (accepting eventual consistency)
items.explain: NoSQL systems usually favour Availability + Partition tolerance, relaxing strong consistency to eventual consistency. Traditional SQL/ACID systems emphasise Consistency.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 24.6)** How does 'consistency' in CAP differ from 'consistency' in ACID?
options: CAP consistency = all replicas show the same value; ACID consistency = a transaction preserves integrity constraints
CAP is about transactions; ACID about replicas
items.explain: CAP-consistency concerns agreement among replicated copies; ACID-consistency concerns a single transaction keeping the database's integrity constraints valid. Same word, different meanings.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 24.14–24.15)** In the graph-oriented NoSQL system Neo4j, data is modelled with nodes and relationships, and its query language is:
items.explain: Neo4j models entities as nodes (with labels and properties) connected by directed relationships; queries use the Cypher (CQL) declarative pattern-matching language (CREATE/MATCH/RETURN).
